workOns.name: Trail knee straightens
workOns.goal: Keep the flex in your trail knee
workOns.saw: Your trail leg straightens going back — on all 10 swings, steady from first swing to last. Typical trail-knee bend lost by the top: 22°, against a target of less than 12°.
workOns.why: A straight trail leg lets your hips slide instead of turn, so you lose power.
workOns.cameWith: It often drags other habits in with it. Not today — on every swing, your head stays level going back, your hips turn in place going back and your hips hold their height going back.

causes.lead: One possible cause showed up on the same swings. Because both happened on every swing, we can't prove one drives the other — so here is what we spotted, what we couldn't check, and what we've ruled out.

rows.title: What we spotted
items: The ball comes off the face slower than usual for you with this club — on 10 of 10 swings, work-on 2
The club drops under the plane and gets stuck behind you coming down — on 10 of 10 swings, work-on 3
The club catches the top of the ball and it runs along the ground — on 10 of 10 swings, work-on 4

drills.label: Trail hip load and hold
drills.instruction: Take your address position, make a slow backswing turn, and stop at the top. Feel the pressure in the trail hip socket rather than on the outside of the trail foot. Hold for three seconds, then return.
drills.targets: To feel the trail hip accepting the turn instead of the pelvis sliding away from the target.
drills.note: The stick is a feedback aid, not the drill. If the hip cannot rotate internally, the slide is the body finding the only route it has.
drills.equipment: an alignment stick outside the trail hip, optional

workOns.cue: As you turn back, feel your trail knee stay soft and pointing at the ball while your trail pocket turns behind you.
workOns.check: Film from down the line. At the top, your trail knee should look about as bent as it did at address.
workOns.target: Trail-knee bend lost by the top: less than 12°, on most swings. Today: 22°.
workOns.figureLabel: Each dot is one swing: trail-knee bend lost by the top, in degrees.

stills.caption: Address, swing 5
stills.note: Your typical swing (swing 5). The line is your trail leg, hip to knee to ankle.

workOns.kicker: Work-on 1 of 5  ·  P4, at the top  ·  10 of 10 swings
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Trail knee straightens, or “standing up on it going back”.

workOns.name: Hips under-rotated at impact
workOns.goal: Have your hips open at impact
workOns.saw: Your hips haven't turned enough by impact — on all 10 swings, steady from first swing to last. Typical hip turn at impact: 3°, against a target of 18° to 58°.
workOns.why: Hips that haven't turned enough get in your arms' way, so your hands take over and the strike varies.

drills.label: Impact hold
drills.instruction: Make slow swings to impact and stop there. Check three things: your belt buckle points between the ball and the target, your trail heel is just off the ground, and your hands are level with your lead thigh. Hold for two seconds, then finish the swing slowly.
drills.targets: To feel where your hips need to be when the club reaches the ball, so the turn has somewhere to go.
drills.note: If your hips will not open without your shoulders opening too, that is a mobility question before it is a practice one.
drills.equipment: a mirror or a phone on a stand

workOns.cue: Through the ball, feel your belt buckle already facing between the ball and the target.
workOns.check: Film face-on. At impact you should see the front of your lead hip, with your belt turned toward the target.
workOns.target: Hip turn at impact: 18° to 58°, on most swings. Today: 3°.
workOns.figureLabel: Each dot is one swing: hip turn at impact, in degrees.

stills.caption: Typical, swing 5
stills.note: Every swing looked much like this one.

workOns.kicker: Work-on 2 of 5  ·  P7, at impact  ·  10 of 10 swings
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Hips under-rotated at impact, or “hips not clearing”, “blocked”.

workOns.name: Early extension
workOns.goal: Stay in your posture through the ball
workOns.saw: You stand up through the ball — on all 10 swings, steady from first swing to last. Typical posture lost by impact: 12.9°, against a target of less than 5°.
workOns.why: Standing up takes away the room your arms need, so your hands have to rescue the strike.
workOns.cameWith: It came with club returns toe-up at impact (7 of the 7 swings we could see). That fits the coaching model, though showing up together is not proof that one causes the other. And on every swing, you lean slightly away from the target at impact.

drills.label: Rod along the spine
drills.instruction: Hold an alignment stick along your spine, touching the back of your head, your upper back and your tailbone. Rehearse your address position and your backswing turn keeping all three in contact.
drills.targets: To feel the spine angle you set at address being kept through the turn.
drills.note: A fixed upper-back curve will stop all three touching. That is information, not a failure.

drills.label: Standoff check
drills.instruction: Set up with a headcover just outside the toe of the club and make swings without hitting it.
drills.targets: To keep the distance between the body and the ball the same at impact as it was at address.
drills.note: The standard first answer to a hosel strike, and it works because it addresses the standoff rather than the fear.

workOns.cue: Keep your backside on an imaginary wall behind you all the way to impact.
workOns.check: Film from down the line with a line drawn down the back of your hips at address. At impact your hips should still be touching it.
workOns.target: Posture lost by impact: less than 5°, on most swings. Today: 12.9°.
workOns.figureLabel: Each dot is one swing: posture lost by impact, in degrees.

stills.caption: At impact, swing 3
stills.note: Orange: your spine at impact. White dashes: the same swing at address. Every swing looked much like this one.

workOns.kicker: Work-on 3 of 5  ·  P7, at impact  ·  10 of 10 swings
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Early extension, or “standing up”, “hip thrust toward the ball”.

workOns.name: Over the top
workOns.goal: Bring your hands down inside the path they went up
workOns.saw: Your hands come over the top coming down — on all 10 swings, steady from first swing to last. Typical hand rise coming down: 11% hand rise, against a target of 9% hand rise or less.
workOns.why: When the club comes over the top it cuts across the ball, so shots start left or curve right.
workOns.cameWith: It often drags other habits in with it. Not today — on every swing, you keep your arms wide at the top.

causes.lead: One possible cause showed up on the same swings. Because both happened on every swing, we can't prove one drives the other — so here is what we spotted, what we couldn't check, and what we've ruled out.

Your upper and lower body don't separate coming down — on 10 of 10 swings, work-on 1

drills.label: Gate drill
drills.instruction: Place two tees, or a headcover just outside the ball, so the club has to travel through a gate to reach it. Start with slow half swings.
drills.targets: To feel the club approaching from a different direction, with immediate feedback when it does not.
drills.note: Set the gate for the path you want, not against the one you have — a gate that punishes the current swing without offering another produces a flinch, not a change.

drills.label: Pump to delivery
drills.instruction: Swing to the top, then move down to about waist height and stop, checking that the shaft is on the plane it started on and your hands still have their angle. Return to the top and repeat three times, then hit the shot.
drills.targets: To rehearse the delivery position rather than to arrive at it by accident.
drills.note: Rehearsal, not a swing thought. Trying to do this consciously at full speed produces a different, slower swing.

workOns.cue: Start down by letting your trail elbow drop toward your trail hip pocket.
workOns.check: Film from down the line. Coming down, your hands should drop below the line they went up on.
workOns.target: Hand rise coming down: 9% hand rise or less, on most swings. Today: 11% hand rise.
workOns.figureLabel: Each dot is one swing: hand rise coming down, in percent of hand rise.
workOns.kicker: Work-on 4 of 5  ·  P6, coming down  ·  10 of 10 swings
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Over the top, or “coming over it”, “OTT”.

workOns.name: Reverse spine angle at P4
workOns.goal: Lean slightly away from the target at the top
workOns.also: “leaning left at the top”, “forward spine angle at the top”
workOns.saw: You lean toward the target at the top — on 9 of 10 swings, steady from first swing to last. Typical lean away from the target at the top: −1°, against a target of 0° to 24°; this is a small miss: just outside the range, never far.
workOns.why: Leaning toward the target at the top strains your lower back and makes it hard to start down smoothly.

causes.lead: One possible cause showed up on the same swings. Because both happened on every swing, we can't prove one drives the other — so here is what we spotted, what we couldn't check, and what we've ruled out.

The ball slices, curving hard away from the target — on 10 of 10 swings, work-on 3

drills.label: Club across the chest
drills.instruction: Without a ball, hold a club across your chest. Turn to the top and check in a mirror that the shaft tilts down toward the target and your chest sits behind the ball. Ten slow turns.
drills.targets: To feel the upper body staying behind the ball as it turns, rather than tipping toward the target.
drills.note: A short turn often hides inside this one: if the shoulders cannot turn further, the body tips instead.

workOns.cue: At the top, feel your sternum stay over your trail thigh.
workOns.check: Film face-on. At the top your head and chest should sit a little behind the ball, never toward the target.
workOns.target: Lean away from the target at the top: 0° to 24°, on most swings. Today: −1°.
workOns.figureLabel: Each dot is one swing: lean away from the target at the top, in degrees.
workOns.kicker: Work-on 5 of 5  ·  P4, at the top  ·  9 of 10 swings
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Reverse spine angle at P4, or “leaning left at the top”, “forward spine angle at the top”.

steps.head: Rehearse without a ball
steps.body: Slow swings, ten at a time, feeling the change. This is where the new move is learned.

steps.head: Small swings with a ball
steps.body: Half swings at half speed. Keep the feel; ignore where the ball goes.

steps.head: Mix it in
steps.body: Full swings: one with the feel, then two normal ones. Film every fifth swing.

steps.head: One thing at a time
steps.body: Stay with work-on 1 until your next session. The rest of the list waits.

numbers.note: Path, face and offline: positive is right of target, negative left (right-handed golfer). Habits: how many of your five work-ons showed on that swing. Typical: the middle value of your ten swings.

about.dates: This report covers your session on Tuesday 20 October 2026 and was prepared on 20 October 2026. If a session is re-analysed, the report is prepared again and carries the new date.
about.measured: 10 swings with a 7 iron, filmed down-the-line and face-on at high frame rate, with every ball measured by a GC Quad. Your body positions are read from the video by pose tracking; the club and ball numbers come from the launch monitor.
about.ranges: Each habit is judged against a target range. Most ranges are coaching judgement, set from what good ball-strikers do; a few come from published measurements. They are not fitted to you. A swing outside the range is not a mistake in itself — it is where the evidence points.
about.notChecked: Some things could not be checked on every swing: pelvis peak a spike (10 of 10); chest peak out of sight (10 of 10); club peak drawn, not judged (10 of 10). Nothing in this report depends on them.
